While much of this damage happened in the eastern side of the city – on streets including La Salle, Huntleigh, Indian, Lexford, and Estates – trees were also down on Monte, Lower Grand, Sunnyside, Hazel Lane, and in Dracena Park. articles.text: After a three-year absence due to COVID, the famed Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will return to Piedmont High School on Thursday, March 30, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. With the theme of “Maskarade,” guests are encouraged to show their creativity and wear bird-themed masks. Created in 1963, by PHS science teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck, the Bird Calling Contest grew into an annual event that over the decades has attracted national and international attention. The winners appeared for many years on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson, and then on Late Night with David Letterman. A panel of judges has been selected to consider the merits of the contestants based upon authenticity of call, poise and delivery, and content of contestants’ introduction of their bird. The judges include: • Rosemary Orozco, Weather forecaster KTVU • Michael Poryes, Television Producer • Joe Fendel, 1991 Bird Calling Contest winner • Jamie Mockel, PHS English teacher • Irma Munoz, PHS Vice Principal Serving as celebrity judges will be Rosemary Orozco, a meteorologist at KTVU, and Michael Poryes, a 1982 PHS grad who created the popular television series “Hannah Montana.” Orozco taught at San Francisco State University and has worked as a meteorologist, journalist and news anchor for several stations. She also has worked as a model and has her own fashion line in San Francisco. Poryes is a three-time Emmy nominee who was an original member of the creative team that developed and launched “Saved by the Bell.” Joe Fendel was a four-time bird caller 1988-91. Glancing through a large plate glass window I saw men, dressed in rough clothes, most wearing hats, seated on wooden benches, not unlike church pews, waiting for what I assume now was work. What caught my attention as I gazed through the window was that almost to a man they were reading newspapers, held like white sails, all lost in that day’s news, a haze of smoke from cigars, pipes and cigarettes drifting above them. articles.text: Earlier this month the Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD) voted to end the sale of new gas furnaces and gas water heaters as early as 2027. The rules are meant to reduce air pollution and target nitrogen oxides (NOx) from gas heating appliances, which can cause respiratory issues and smog. According to BAAQMD, up to 85 premature deaths caused by air pollution will be avoided each year due to the new rules. The appliance standard will also reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In Piedmont, residential buildings account for 49% of greenhouse gas emissions, with the overwhelming share of these emissions coming from natural gas used for heating and cooling. What does this mean for Piedmonters? After 2027, if your gas water heater breaks and cannot be repaired, you’ll need to replace it with an electric one. The same goes for gas furnaces starting in 2029. While heat pumps and heat pump water heaters can be costly upfront, many rebates are available to offset the price. Earlier this year, the City of Piedmont launched an electrification rebate program, which offers an $800 rebate for heat pump water heaters, a $750- $1,500 rebate for heat pumps, and a $500 rebate for panel upgrades. To learn more, visit the Rebates and Incentives page on the City’s Planning and Building Department website at bit.ly/3JSLwxQ. Rebates available from other organizations such as BayREN and California Energy Smart Homes can be stacked on top of the City’s rebates for maximum savings. Visit SwitchIsOn.org to see what rebates you qualify for. At the federal level, the High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate Program, created by the Inflation Reduction Act, will provide an upfront rebate of up to $8,000 for heat pumps, a $1,750 rebate for heat pump water heaters, and a $4,000 rebate for electrical system upgrades. The program is anticipated to launch next year. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions. articles.text: As excavation work continues at the Piedmont Community Pool construction site, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that recent storms have delayed the original schedule by an estimated four weeks, mainly due to PG&E delays. He was optimistic that the contractor, Wickman Development & Construction, could work with the city to “mitigate the delay and gain time back.” With 335 working days (including adjustments for weather) assigned to Wickman when the project began on January 19, the project was originally estimated to finish in late spring or early summer in 2024. Excavation work is expected to continue into late spring and has been more difficult due to rainstorms as water accumulates in the holes cut in bedrock for the foundation of a new main and medium-sized pool. To prevent flooding, Gonzales said the contractors have been busy pumping the water out “through tanks, or to filter it through a series of what [the EPA] calls Best Management Practices. They don’t pump directly into storm drains.” However, the biggest storm-related challenge has been PG&E. articles.text: Scouting volunteers will be recognized at the Piedmont Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner on Thursday, March 30, in the Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Tickets are $55, with a reception at 6 p.m. and dinner and awards beginning at 7 p.m. “Our volunteers support our local youth development, and provide service to the greater community as well,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “They are guiding these youth through service projects that impact our community right now, such as Scouting for Food, creek clean ups, and more. But their impacts also continue for decades, as today’s Scouts carry the ethic of service throughout their lifetime.” The Silver Beaver Award, the highest recognition a council can give a volunteer, will be presented to longtime Scout volunteer Chris Lee. articles.text: The Piedmont High Affinity Mentorship class, in collaboration with the Piedmont Education Foundation, held a student speaker and panel discussion, “Creating a Culture of Belonging,” in the Alan Harvey theater, Monday, March 20. Students shared their experiences of “othering” within Piedmont and the school district with an audience of nearly 200 community members. Three student speakers and a panel of 10 students of various religious, ethnic, and racial backgrounds, gender identities, and nationalities explained the ways in which microaggressions, slurs and social hierarchies within Piedmont have left them feeling unsafe and uncomfortable within their own skin. The speakers included seniors Morgan Hunt, Sohrab Ford and Stephanie Tsung, alongside panelist Danny Allen, Meher Bachher, Sofia Prieto Black, Adelina Mbise, Cole Nash, Dahlia Saffouri, and Elena Stevens. English teacher and teacher union president Dr. Elise Marke commended the success of the event during a school board meeting on Wednesday March 22. “The words said on that stage really need to be heard by every parent, teacher and staff member, administrator and community member in this city,” said Marks. Student presenters shared stories and experiences about facing alienation from classmates, and the negative impact it had on their sense of self. “Although it may not be the blunt racism such as saying the n-word to my face, but the subtleties of simply leaving me out, or making sure that I knew what set me apart from everyone else was heartbreaking,” Morgan Hunt said in her speech Monday night, “It completely ruined the way that I saw myself, it made me grow to become ashamed of my Blackness, I didn’t want to be the exception, I just wanted to be me.” Hunt has given multiple speeches about her experiences in Piedmont, and is upset by the lack of change, even as these topics continue to be brought to light by students. “It’s frustrating that we have to keep on talking about this topic and the culture hasn’t changed. A lot of people that go to Piedmont might never have to interact with minorities….and that’s a big problem,” Hunt added. Stephanie Tsung’s speech portrayed unique perspective, moving from somewhere she was the majority and fit in, to being othered in Piedmont. “I moved from Hong Kong, where the majority is Asian, and so I fit in pretty well. But after moving to Piedmont, I was able to experience certain things that I hadn’t before,” said Tsung. “The little things people said, made me feel like I’m not one of them, or that I’m different or I didn’t belong here.” Tsung believes these racist statements often come from ignorance, rather than an intent to be harmful. “Intent and impact aren’t always aligned, but people need to be more aware of their words. I think a lot of the time it’s just ignorance,” said Tsung. Panelist Meher Bachher, a freshman, believes that more administrative accountability would encourage students to understand the impact of their words and actions. “A lot of the problems are perpetuated by lack of administrative accountability, and lack of action. When a student does something wrong, instead of helping them understand the consequences of their actions, the incident as a whole is just brushed under the rug,” said Bachher. articles.text: Lake Merritt, the beloved jewel in the center of Oakland, is in jeopardy. Recent events do not bode well for the future of the city’s home to waterfowl, joggers, and dog lovers. For decades, the Lake Merritt Institute, a community oriented nonprofit sponsored by a contract with the City of Oakland and with donations from supporters, has worked to keep the downtown estuary clean by empowering volunteers to remove trash. But now, problems are threatening to overwhelm the lake, and the needs are many. Last summer (2022) a red toxic algae bloom triggered water oxygen levels to drop to zero. A fish kill resulted in 10,000 fish dying and washing up on the shoreline. Even if the two city contracts proposed for 2023-2024 are approved, that funding would not meet requirements to keep Lake Merritt clean. To combat Lake Merritt’s problems, the Lake Merritt Institute has established a gofundme campaign at: Gofundme.com/f/help-save-lakemerritt-and-lake-merritt-institute. So far, $14,533 has been raised toward a goal of $150,000. The Funds will be used for: • A fourth water quality monitoring buoy to be deployed in the channel through which tidal water enters and exits the lake. This buoy would be deployed for a year to measure nutrients and other data necessary to design a system to prevent future fish kills. Goal: $20,000. • An electric quad utility vehicle to replace an old truck, and to be used to haul bags of trash removed from the lake. Goal: $22,000 • Accounting and tax preparation services, and updated accounting software. Goal: $5,000. • Staff assistance to maintain social media accounts, help prepare the newsletter, maintain bulletin boards, and monitor water quality. Goal: $73,000. • New nets, trash bags, barrels, as well as protective gear such as gloves and boots. Goal: $4,000. • Three shallow water aerators to replace fountains where depth is now too shallow to operate, and which will create islands of oxygenated water where fish can find refuge during fish kills. Goal: $18,000. In addition, major funding is needed for a lake-wide aeration and oxygenation system that would prevent future fish kills. This system will be designed in 2023, and costs could be as high as $2,000,000. For further information, contact LMI Executive Director James Robinson at 238-2290, or see Lakemerrittinstitute.org. Since December 1996 the institute has been removing between 1,000 and 6,000 pounds of trash from the lake each month under a contract with the City of Oakland. Much of the work is done by volunteers. articles.text: The Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present an evening of Short Films on April 20 at 7:00 p.m. at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on the Havens School campus at 325 Highland Avenue. Help the Appreciating Diversity Film Series enrich the Piedmont Food Fest’s celebration of Bay Area diversity with five family friendly films that will explore the many flavors of families. Bring your family and friends and experience the range of family diversity through themes such as adoption, homelessness, women’s issues, education, and gender identity. The films are appropriate for children ages 10 and up. As always, Diversity films are free. A list of films that will be screened starting at 7:00 p.m. are listed below in the order in which they will be shown. The total running time for all five films is about one hour. • Absolutely No Spitting A Jewish mother and her multiracial 4-year-old adopted daughter explore their DNA profiles and what it means to have many identities and cultures in your genetic heritage. • A Concerto Is a Conversation A virtuoso jazz pianist and film composer traces his family’s lineage through his 91-year-old grandfather from Jim Crow laws in Florida to the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles. The grandfather describes the development of his love for music as well as his ingenious methods of getting ahead that made it possible for his family to thrive then and for coming generations. • Almost Famous: The Silent Pulse of the Universe In 1967, a young astronomer, Jocelyn Bell, made a breakthrough discovery in astronomy, but as a woman in the sciences her role was overlooked and unfairly ignored. While Jocelyn was belittled and sexually harassed by the media, the Nobel Prize was awarded to her professor and his boss. • What You’ll Remember The story of young Bay Area parents determined to give their four children a good life despite moving in and out of homelessness over a period of fifteen years. While the family waited for stable, affordable housing, they nurtured and educated their children in resourceful, inspiring ways, creating a feeling of “home” even when there was no house. • Texas Strong Kai Shappley, a 6-year-old trans child in Texas, fights to be recognized and accepted by her devout Christian family. Kai’s mother, Shirley, must deal with her church, while Kai navigates life at school, where she is banned from the girls’ bathroom. Winner of the 2018 Emmy for Outstanding Short Documentary. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series is co-sponsored by Piedmont School District, the City of Piedmont, the Oakland and Piedmont Leagues of Women Voters, and the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee. articles.text: Twenty-one Piedmont High School journalism students attended Columbia Scholastic Press Association’s Spring Convention fro March 15-17 at Columbia University in New York City. After lectures, workshops, and discussions, the students returned home with new ideas for improvements for the school news magazine, The Piedmont Highlander (TPH). The PHS students were chaperoned by newspaper advisor and English Department Chair Beth Black, and former PHS science teacher Tom Huffaker. articles.text: If you research speech and language development, you will find many references to “word count”. “Word count”, although not the entire speech/language developmental picture, is often used as a quick and easy measure of a child’s developing communication profile. Beginning as early as the 12- or 18- month pediatrician visit, you will likely be asked about your child’s current “word count”. Developmental norms suggest 3–5 words at age 12 months, and 20–50 words at 18 months. How do those first words magically appear? And what can we do if they do not? We can look earlier and deeper than the “word count” for the answers. Learning to talk starts long before a child says their first words. First words are built upon four layers: understanding, interacting, gesturing and making sounds. The foundation for speaking words is understanding words. You cannot use a word correctly if you do not completely understand it. There is a gap between how many words children understand and how many they can produce, with the words understood outnumbering the words used. A suggestion is to hold up items as you talk about them or point to pictures in books as you say the word, so the child can focus on learning the meaning of words. articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn The Highlander girls’ lacrosse team beat Berkeley 13-8 on Friday, March 24 at Witter Field. Piedmont lost 13-12 in double overtime loss to the Yellowjackets in last year’s Western Alameda County Conference playoff semifinals. “We just asked the girls to focus, keep really good communication, trusting each other, and playing as a team. We have a pretty young team, and we found it’s taking a little bit of time for everyone to come together. So far this season, we’ve seen some really good halves, but tonight I thought we played a full game,” said assistant coach Greg Tschider, who was filling in for coach Carlton Chan on Friday. It was a strong offensive performance for Ruby Guzdar and Molly Ashton, who combined for seven goals. “On offense, Ruby is really quick. There are certain players who know how to get to goal and put it in the back of the net, and Ruby is one of those players. We really look to Molly and Eleanor [Lavin] to provide leadership on offense, keep us controlled, and focused. It was an aggressive game by both teams, this game was ultimately won by the team that got more ground balls and who had fewer turnovers,” said Tschider. Ruby Guzdar (3) scored four goals against Berkeley. Game Recap Piedmont jumped out quickly to hold a commanding 5-1 advantage by halftime. They added seven more goals and conceded seven after intermission. The Highlanders led 3-0 before Berkeley scored its first goal. Guzdar opened scoring eight minutes into play, then Friedie Schickendanz scored a minute and a half later with 15:55 remaining. Guzdar scored again nearly 30 seconds later. Berkeley made it 3-1 with 10:51 left in the half, but it was the only time they’d get on the scoreboard in the opening 25 minutes. From there, Ashton scored her first goal with 7:19 to go and then Eleanor Lavin netted one with 3:23 left. Piedmont’s win over Berkeley puts them in second-place of the Western Alameda County Conference. Molly Ashton had a hat trick against the Yellowjacktes. In the second half, the two sides traded goals all the way until the end—scoring seven apiece. Berkeley scored 30 seconds into the action, but 18 answered a minute later and Guzdar got her hat trick after another 40 seconds. 2 made it 8-3 with 19:36 to go, and then Piedmont went up 10-3 with a pair of goals by Ashton. Berkeley then scored three consecutive times to make it 10-6 with 9:38 left in the game. After back-and-forth possessions, PHS’ Guzdar scored her fourth goal with 5:52 left and 14 added one with 5:05 remaining. The Jackets netted one with three minutes to go, but 18 scored Piedmont’s 13th goal with 2:18 remaining. Berkeley scored the game’s final goal with 1:19 on the clock. Final stats: Guzdar scored four goals, recovered three loose balls, and won five draws. Ashton had three goals. Lavin had one goal, two ground balls, and won two draws. Watson scored twice and won two draws. Bentley scored once and had two ground balls. Schickendanz scored once and had two assists. Graham had a goal and assist. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team swept past North Coast Section foe Lick-Wilmerding 7-0 at home on Wednesday, March 22, setting the stage for a closer margin of victory two days later against Bishop O’Dowd, 4-3, in a match March 24 at Merritt College. “We had a victorious week. We are just about at full strength with Ben [Breber] back in action. I think our quality dipped a bit after the win over Lick-Wilmerding, but we still won a close match against O’Dowd,” said coach Jim Landes. Wednesday’s win over Lick featured No. 2 singles starter Ben Breber, a junior, returning to the lineup after missing all but one match this season due to illness. He won both his matches, defeating Lick’s Este Ciu 6-4, 7-5, and O’Dowd’s Colin Sweeney 6-3, 6-4. “It feels so good to be back out here – especially for the team. It hasn’t been just me missing time; people have been in and out of the lineup. It felt really good to come out at full strength against a good team,” said Breber after winning the clinching fourth match against Lick. Breber showed his usual array of thunderous forehands and serves to overpower his opponents. No. 1 singles starter Lucas Smolko, a freshman, continued his impressive debut season with a pair of wins, beating Soahil Mishra of Lick 6-4, 6-3, O’Dowd’s Neo Chai, 6-2, 6-3. Smolko is a 3-star nationally ranked recruit who is competing on a team environment for the first time in his tennis career. “It’s a little more pressure, Staff Photos Freshman Lucas Smolko talks about the nuances of tournament tennis compared to high school team play. but it’s a really cool environment where I get to have teammates and we can support each other. Tennis is a really solitary sport, so it’s nice to have that difference. With high school matches, you’re feeling pressure to win for your team as opposed to just yourself,” Smolko explained. 7-0 shutout vs. Lick-Wilmerding In singles, Smolko won 6-4, 6-3 at the No. 1 spot while Breber won 6-4, 7-5 at No. 2. Ethan Pham won handily at No. 3 with scores of 6-0, 6-1, and Brady Colbert won 6-4, 6-2 at No. 4. At No,1 doubles, Nate Welch and Monte Imburg went to three sets before winning, 6-3, 5-7, 10-7. Playing No.2, Arun Brahma and Nick King also won in three sets, 6-4, 5-7, 10-3. Will Tenney and Graham Alban at No, 3 closed out the match in two sets, winning 6-4, 6-4. Ben Breber made his return to Piedmont High after missing several matches this season due to an illness. He won both matches last week at No. 2 singles. Monte Imburg and Nate Welch won their matches in three sets against Lick Wilmerding and Bishop O’Dowd.

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum currently is exhibiting Color Trip: Yoshida Hodaka’s Modern Prints, the first ever solo exhibition of the artist in the United States. His exhibit showcases the Japanese printmaker’s influential craft. Hodaka, a native of Tokyo, was an influential figure of postWorld War II Japanese printmaking. Born in 1926, he is known for his abstract and colorful prints. Hodaka included surreal landscapes and abstract forms in his art, which is inspired by photography, poetry, and ancient art. “Hodaka was a rebel in the best sense – someone who imagined a new way of seeing the world,” explained the exhibition organizer Yuki Morishima, associate curator of Japanese art at the Asian Art Museum. “By combining the centuries-old woodblock printing with the modern methods of photo etching and collage and contemporary influences like Pop art and foreign travel, Hodaka opened up a new frontier in Japanese printmaking that was completely original to him.” Hodaka’s collection of a dozen poster-size prints, Zodiac Landscape (1973), is on view, as well as his sketchbooks and a collection of artwork made by his family members. “Hodaka playfully assembled and juxtaposed ordinary objects out of context, creating his surreal scenes with dreamlike atmospheres. Every time you look at these prints, you find something new and exciting hiding in the landscape,” Morishima said. The exhibition will be on view through May 1. articles.text: All Quiet on the Western Front won the 2023 Academy Award for Best International film. All Quiet on the Western Front is extraordinary, beautifully photographed and acted, nominated for nine Oscars at the recent 95th Academy Awards and the winner of the Best International film. It is based on Eric Remarque’s 1929 classic anti-war novel of the same name, and it could be argued that its contemporary context is today’s war in Ukraine. The narrative opens with Paul Baumer (Frank Krammer) marching in a long line of new recruits. They are headed toward the front, filled with patriotic eagerness, singing a song, filled with German patriotism, unaware of the carnage that awaits them. Each is wearing a uniform salvaged from a dead soldier, freshly laundered, the bullet holes patched. But soon, for these young men, and countless others, the agony and finality of war will become a reality. The camera follows Paul, running through the icy water of the trenches, claustrophobic warrens filled with pools of blood and shattered bodies. Before long his spirit is crushed and the look in his eyes is now vacant, his face twisted with fear, the optimistic rationale for the war lost to him, replaced only with his will to survive. In one chilling scene Paul stabs a French soldier and then sits next to him as he slowly dies. Sitting in a bomb crater, his face in his hands, he is overwhelmed by what he has done, grieving for his lost humanity. Meanwhile, far from the front, the French and German powers sit across from one another, attempting to negotiate a cease-fire, fully aware that while the hours pass hundreds are maimed or killed by withering gunfire and explosives. The world watched then as the casualties mounted, much as it does today, and the futility of it all, the frightful unyielding tragedy of war continues as history repeats itself. Peter Jackson’s much acclaimed documentary, They Shall Not Grow Old, also a profound and detailed look at the horrors of World War I from an English perspective.
articles.title: All Quiet on the Western Front - profound, unforgettable

articles.text: What Peter Jackson has accomplished in They Shall Not Grow Old is extraordinary, bordering on the magical. Given access to hundreds of hours of World War I archival news footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum, he began what was to be a 30-minute short. It ultimately morphed into an astonishing, years-long restorative achievement. Using computer-generated, state-of-the-art technology Jackson undertook what was a meticulous cleaning of the dusty, scratched, grainy film. Realizing that the footage was hand cranked and had been shot at various speeds, he synched it up to a standard 24-frames-per-second. Then he and his talented cohort began the painstaking process of colorization in which the restorers went to astonishing lengths to achieve accuracy. They included trips to actual locations where they shot countless reference photos. Then they created a soundtrack that is spot-on, In images where soldiers are speaking, they hired lip readers to determine what was said and hired local actors to get the accents just right. No narration was used; rather they listened to some 600 hours of BBC recordings of WWI veterans and used 100 voices. We hear them reflecting on their experiences, offering their memories absent even a hint of cynicism. The result is almost surreal. It’s as if we are literally stepping back in time and observing from the camera’s point of view what is taking place. The story is told chronologically, beginning with contextual images shot in black and white of enlistees (some as young as 14 years-old) arriving at boot camp as civilians and then gradually turned into disciplined soldiers. We learn through voice-overs that to a man they believed they were embarking on an unrivaled adventure, one not to be missed, wrapped in patriotism and heroism and a promise that the war would end within months. England vibrated with war fever. Train stations were filled with cheering, f lag waving crowds saying goodbye. Men on the streets of London not yet in uniform, were often approached by young women who handed them white feathers, symbols of cowardice, urging them to join their comrades. On walls and buildings were posters, appealing to men (and boys) to enlist and do their part. It’s at this point in the narrative that the screen fills with color and we, the audience, begin in earnest to comprehend that what Jackson has done is create a work of art. We are there. All but shoulder to shoulder with these young men who soon came to realize that the much-anticipated adventure proves to be an unimaginable ordeal, harsh, stark, all but unendurable. The young Brits found that this was a war fought from the warrens of crooked trenches, often filled with the stench of death, filled with water and partially buried bodies, blackened hands and arms sticking out of layers of mud. To confront the enemy meant climbing up and over the top, onto the field of battle, often into withering machine gun fire and exploding shells, later spending nights trying to sleep in shallow hollowed out caves while an unrelenting bombardment from Germans shook the ground. For many this adventure became life maiming or life ending. And those who stopped and looked into the box-like cameras, gave stoic smiles or long gazes of brittle confidence; in truth they knew what was ahead. World War I (1914-1918) was referred to as “The War to End All Wars.” After watching They Shall Not Grow Old, it is clear why it was unimaginable that such carnage would ever be repeated. The toll was staggering, 5,500,000 men were killed, and an additional 12 million wounded. Poison gas was used, inflicting 1.3 million casualties. Civilian deaths totaled over 4 million. And 1 million British boys were killed. The loss for a small island nation was incomprehensible. At no time during They Shall Not Grow Old is there any commentary by Jackson or others about the nature of war. And yet, after the last frame fades from the screen, it is all but impossible not to conclude that what was created is an anti-war film. To see WWI as it was, while knowing that the horror was far worse (the archival footage was meant for audiences back in England), is revelatory. And, of course, embedded in the 99-minute film is the haunting question: why does war seem to be ever with us? They Shall Not Grow Old. WWI Documentary. articles.text: Ghost in the Shell is a live action remake of the classic Japanese anime film created by Mamoru Oshii in 1995. When it was made it was considered visionary, even revolutionary and explored the nexus between robotics/computers and sentient beings. Embedded in its narrative was the question that if we begin to merge with sophisticated machines, how will that merger ultimately affect our essential humanity? Ghost is a familiar, big budget, Hollywood epic starring Scarlett Johansson as Major Mira, a hybrid human whose brain (meaning her “Ghost”) was inserted into a cyborg body after a catastrophic accident. She has emerged as a relentless warrior working for the government (Section 9) tracking criminals and terrorists. The immediate problem with Ghost is not its astonishing CGI visuals – in fact it is so amazing to look at it almost seems to be a computer graphics vanity film. What it lacks is any kind of narrative coherence. It’s as if the writers assume that they can drop act one, meaning any exposition that explains who, what and where, and simply begin the story as if all that came before simply doesn’t matter. That may be a reasonable assumption if the audience is familiar with the earlier Ghost. But if the story is new to the Scarlett Johansson as Major Mira Killian in Ghost in the Shell filmgoer, then this predicate only causes confusion. I assume that since this remake was not done in stateof-the-art anime, the filmmakers believed that an American audience would embrace a film that in many ways is similar to the iconic Ridley Scott film, Blade Runner, where the post-human cyborgs are called replicants. Like Blade, the world in Ghost is dystopian, Asian in setting, though not in characters, and densely populated. The interactions in Blade, however, are far more interesting and the question of gauging the authenticity of the characters (human or replicant) is embedded in the story until the last scene. As an aside, anime (a shortening of animation) as a genre, as an art form, is hugely popular in Japan. Wikipedia describes anime as “possessing a certain style characterized by colorful graphics, vibrant characters, and fantastical themes… It combines graphic art, cinematography, and other forms of imaginative techniques, to include large, emotive eye size.” Assuming that the remake of Ghost represents collaborations between Hollywood and Japanese studios, it is unfortunate that the original Mamoru Oshii story was allowed so little opportunity to develop. But then, when it comes to films of this sci-fi/futuristic genre, Hollywood action will always trump that which is more philosophical. Ghost in the Shell. Directed by Rupert Sanders. articles.text: Reese Witherspoon and Pico Alexander star in Home Again If you enjoy romantic comedies (rom-coms), then it’s likely you’ve seen one of Nancy Meyers’ films dating back as far as Baby Boom or Something’s Gotta Give. Or perhaps you saw It’s Complicated or The Holiday. Meyers was and still remains a filmmaker who found a niche and perfected it. Her world in film is as light as a wedding shower balloon, so enticingly surreal that it qualifies as pure warm-hearted escapism. And now here is Meyers’ daughter, Hallie Meyers-Shyer, debuting with Home Again, written and directed by Hallie and in almost all ways a mirror of the genre staked out by her mom. This film stars Reese Witherspoon as Alice, a separated mom, a recent New York transplant to L.A., living with her two daughters in her departed father’s Hollywood Spanish villa cum guesthouse. All is soft California sunshine, blue skies, with a room in the house dedicated to her once famous filmmaker father. Her mom, Lillian, ex-actress, played wonderfully by Candace Bergen, oversees her daughter’s, and granddaughters’ transition. What mom did not plan on was abruptly having three twenty-something aspiring filmmakers win her heart and temporarily living in her guesthouse. One, Harry, portrayed by Pico Alexander, is totally captivated with Alice, no matter the age difference (Alice is 40). As you can imagine, it’s complicated, especially when Alice’s husband, Austen (Michael Sheen), arrives unannounced from New York, hoping to make his case for a second chance in the marriage. The film has its comedic moments as well as a bit of drama for a diversion. It’s also the stuff that makes critics cranky. But if you’re looking for an escape and wishing to spend 97 minutes with some decent, attractive and mannerly people who will make you smile, then this fantasy rom-com is just the answer. Home Again. Starring Reese Witherspoon, Pico Alexander and Candace Bergen. Directed by Hallie Meyers-Shyer. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: the wine loving world knows about Ridge Vineyards. Instead of hailing from Napa or Sonoma Valley, they are perched up on a…well, ridge in Cupertino overlooking Silicon Valley. They also have an outpost in Sonoma County on Lytton Springs Road that gives birth to their iconic old vine Zinfandels. Since the 1960’s when the winery was started by some vino loving Stanford professors, it has been the quintessential American winery – down to the use of American oak barrels rather than French. When I go to France for a home exchange or a special winery visit, I always slip a bottle of Ridge Zinfandel into my suitcase as a gift. “Here,” I proudly say to my French friend, “This is the best we Yanks can do.” One of the things I marvel about is the sheer amount of wines they make. On their website are page after page of different wines available for sale. Many are tiny little lots from a small vineyard they found somewhere and available only through one of their wine clubs. Others are large production wines available all over the country. And the list is always changing. I look forward to the annual new release of wines to see what they will come up with next. This year’s releases include some old stalwarts and some newcomers – all worth checking out. • 2021 Ridge Mancini Ranch This is a new one to me. A blend of 73% Carignane and 27% Zinfandel from the Russian River Valley. Both in France and in America, Carignane is the overlooked step-sister of grapes. Rarely does it play a starring role and is usually considered a backup blending grape. This bottling shows what a charming performer the grape can be. It is elegant and lithe with bright cherry and plum notes. It has great acid and structure and a clean satisfying finish. A perfect wine for grilled burgers. • 2020 Ridge Syrah Grenache Mataro This blend is heavy on Syrah (79%) which makes for a dark, brooding, beefy wine. The Grenache lends bright fruit and the Mataro (Mourvedre) an interesting earthy complexity. It is bursting with blackberry, cassis and leather aromas with tons of luscious dark berry fruit in the mouth. This big, structured wine should last a decade in the cellar. • 2022 Ridge Rose Lytton Estate Wow. My first Ridge Rose. They have made tiny quantities for their wine club in the past, but this is the first national release. Made from Grenache, Zinfandel, Cinsault and Counoise, this light salmon colored wine is bursting with fresh strawberry and fig aromas. Lots of lucious juicy stone fruit on the palate and a clean, refreshing finish. A perfect spring and summer picnic wine. • 2021 Ridge Zinfandel East Bench From a high-altitude vineyard overlooking Dry Creek Valley, this 100% Zinfandel has a bright berry nose, medium body with good acid to give it balance. A very food-friendly type of Zinfandel/ Try it with grilled steaks or chops. • 2021 Ridge Zinfandel Paso Robles From one of Paso’a best vineyards, the Benito Dusi Ranch, this is a huge, brooding wine that floods your mouth with blueberry and blackberry fruit. It has good concentration which leads to a long finish. This Zin should improve in the cellar for 5 years. • 2021 Ridge Chardonnay Ridge is so strongly associated with red wines that its lovely Chardonnay often gets overlooked. Grown up on Montebello ridge next to their esteemed Cabernet grapes, this wine shows perfect acidity and structure. It has an attractive nose of peaches and apples with a touch of baking spices. It finishes long with lingering oak and toast notes. • 2021 Ridge Geyserville Along with Lytton Springs this is Ridge’s flagship Zinfandel blend. articles.text: Thomas D. Clark, a 50-year Piedmont resident with his wife Judie who died in their home May 2022, has entered into an endowment gift agreement with the University of California Berkeley that will provide more than $3 million for UC Berkeley Law School. UC Chancellor Carol T. Christ thanked Clark for his gifts as “remarkable commitments establishing the Thomas David and Judith Swope Clark Current Use Chair in Constitutional Law and the Thomas David and Judith Swope Clark Symposium on Constitutional Interpretation Fund. “We are truly grateful for this extraordinary act of generosity, which will broaden our ability to educate, research, and host engaging and groundbreaking symposia around constitutional law topics,” Chris said. Thomas and Judie grew up in Willits and both graduated from UC Berkeley, Thomas in 1967 and Judie in 1966. In 1972 Thomas graduated from Berkeley Law and in 1975 Judie graduated from Golden Gate Law School. Thomas’s first trial during his initial year of legal practice was in Federal District Court where he successfully defended Oakland Airport regulations that he wrote on expressive activities at the Airport which were challenged by the American Civil Liberty Union. The ACLU did not appeal. Thomas has been a lifelong member of the ACLU and deeply admires the US Constitution and its protection of civil rights and liberties. As his gift Agreement with UC states, “Tom’s purpose in making an endowment to Berkeley Law is especially to support scholarship in US Constitutional law, particularly interpretation of the law as a counterweight to the US Supreme Court’s fatally-flawed, mean and narrow ‘originalism’ policy-driven interpretation.”

His father, Elliott, was married five times and adopted Ford when he was about nine years old. Elliott’s siblings were Anna, James, Franklin Jr, and John. An older brother, Franklin, died as an infant. Ford encouraged the Piedmont Seniors to read some of his father’s works, including the “Eleanor Mysteries”, which include Murder in the Executive Mansion, Murder in the Chateau, Murder in the Map Room, Murder in the Blue Room, and Murder and the First Lady. It began its decline and was seized in San Francisco in 1980 as a front for drug smugglers, and was impounded at Treasure Island, where it unceremoniously sank. articles.text: Elizabeth MacDonald returns to her hometown as co-owner of Grand Lake Vet Dr. Elizabeth MacDonald, a Piedmonter who has co-owned and run the Grand Lake Veterinary Hospital since 2018, spoke with the Post about growing up in Piedmont (Head-Royce Class of 1991), her lifelong love of animals, and her experiences in running the independent veterinary clinic. As one of five MacDonald kids, she said, “I am what one might call a lifer. I have wanted to be a vet my entire life. I think half of Piedmont’s outdoor pets that lived on Wildwood Avenue conveniently ‘followed me home’ when I was a child. I also owned snakes, birds, cats, dogs, chinchillas, rats and hamsters while I was growing up. I am sure if Piedmont had allowed it, there would have been chickens, ducks or goats in there as well.” Her father, Ward, served on the Piedmont School Board. Her mother, Mimi, created the Boosters Club for Piedmont Middle School sports families, and was instrumental in encouraging the editor of this paper to start the Piedmont Post 25 years ago. MacDonald herself majored in biology at Davidson College in North Carolina and graduated from the UC Davis School of Veterinary Medicine in 2000. After completing a one-year internship in New York City at The Animal Medical Centre, she returned to California to practice. At Grand Lake, she and co-owner Dr. Eleanor Dunn manage both an out-patient and in-patient hospital, a pharmacy and a surgical center, and have 45 employees. “There is a reason I spent 20 years trying to find my way back home. Piedmont is a unique community because, despite being in the middle of a huge metropolitan area, it has managed to maintain small community values. As a community, Piedmont is committed to supporting neighbors, friends and families, and in general looking out for one another,” she said. Grand Lake opened in 2013, Piedmont native Elizabeth MacDonald is now a veterinarian and co-owner of Grand Lake Veterinary Hospital on Grand Avenue. and while it has always centered on the care of animals, the staff was especially strained during the pandemic, when pet ownership surged and many veterinary ERs were so overloaded that they had to turn away new patients. “There was a national shortage of vets already due to a shortage of schools and the fact that they’re so expensive,” said MacDonald. “Once the pandemic hit, we never closed, and we did everything we could to see our patients the same day or next day.” “Our staff were tasked with being their best selves at a time when clients were anxious and stressed. We are grateful that Piedmonters were so patient and kind.” Her clinic was further strained when nearby and corporate-owned Montclair Veterinary Hospital closed its doors last April, leaving an estimated patient load of 5,000 without medical care overnight. “That doesn’t happen with individual, privately owned hospitals very often,” MacDonald said. “Vets are part of and serve the communities they live in. I know how deeply these community values are respected in Piedmont. “Since returning home, I get to help pets live better, happier, healthier lives, and help their owners do the same. I’m optimistic that more vets will get back into privately owned, community-centric hospitals,” she added. At the end of the day, said MacDonald, “I do have the best job in the world. Every day, I still get unconditional love and licks from furry patients. My father always used to say, ‘You will spend more time at work than you will with your family, so you must love what you do.’” “I would add to that ‘You must love who you do it with,’” she said.

articles.text: Ancient Egypt meets High Tech in current exhibit of Ramses Fifteen lucky Piedmont Seniors took a trip to San Francisco on Wednesday, February 8, to visit the deYoung Museum in Golden Gate Park and see the unique, extraordinary collection of Egyptian artifacts, including mummies, jewelry and so much more, with 181 ancient relics on display. This exhibition represented the largest collection of Ramses II objects and jewelry to travel to the United States. The exhibit, “Ramses the Great and the Gold of the Pharaohs”, is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to recapture the time of Ramses II, also known as Ramses the Great. Ramses, the most powerful pharaoh, was believed to be a god on earth. He ruled for 67 years, and during his reign, he oversaw the erection of enormous temples, statues and monuments. He even made an idealized statue as a tribute to his mother. There were also newly discovered mummies of animals and treasures from the royal tombs of Dahshur and Tanis. Egyptians believed in an afterlife, and their tombs were filled with valuable artifacts and jewelry that they could use on their next journey. The Seniors walked among the towering statues that re-created moments from Ramses’s life, including his triumph at Kadesh, the largest chariot battle ever fought. The group was provided with personal audio tapes to help them decipher the individual exhibits. Though the hall was crowded, entry to the hall was timed to minimize crowding around the exhibits. One was reminded of a Disney ride where, Ramses the Great gets rock star treatment at SF’s de Young Museum. upon exiting the galleries, visitors came upon the museum’s gift shop, In this case, it was the museum gift shop selling Egyptian souvenirs. In addition, the deYoung has a wonderful selection of books, stationery, jewelry and unusual goods for purchase, comprising two floors of shopping. The exhibition also has a 10-minute optional opportunity to participate in a Virtual Reality show. The more adventurous Seniors who chose to participate in this immersion experience saw Ramses and his wife, Nefertari on the ‘Journey to Osiris’. None of the Seniors had ever experienced this type of show, which could be compared to a Hollywood movie set, only with an Egyptian theme where Nefertari made a loving tribute to her husband, Ramses, with most unusual visual effects. Due to its popularity, both the exhibit and the virtual reality sold out early, and the exhibition closed on February 12. The Seniors worked up a hearty appetite after visiting the exhibits and had boxed unches from the De Young Café waiting for them, avoiding long lines at the café. After leaving the De Young Museum, the group wasn’t quite ready to go home so their accommodating bus driver was willing to serve as a tour guide, pointing out popular spots in the city, including Diamond Heights, the Painted Ladies Victorian houses at Alamo Square, the Castro District, and Mission Bay including Chase Stadium and the UCSF hospital. The Piedmont Seniors hold monthly meetings at the Piedmont Community Hall, typically on fourth Wednesday of each month from 10 a.m. to 12 noon. Monthly excursions travel to a variety of destinations throughout the greater Bay Area. If you would like more information about this active group, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. You do not have to be a Piedmont resident to join in the activities. By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just got a new iMac, and I was wondering if I can still use my old external drive to back it up with Time Machine? The older drive is the same age as my old Mac, about eight-years-old. Also, I seem to remember that when you set it up, you had to format that external drive. If I get a new one, will I have to do the same thing? –Janice D, Oakland Dear Janice: I remember that we ordered you a new iMac, because (besides the fact that the newer operating system would not run on it) your old one was starting to make a lot of noise, clicking, coming from the internal hard drive. This means that the internal hard drive was starting to fail and was probably damaged. So, if you imagine that external hard drives and internal hard drives are the same types of devices, using an eight-year-old external drive with a new machine is probably not a good idea. External hard drives, as well as internal ones, don’t last forever, and there is a saying in the tech world, “it’s not a matter of whether your hard drive will fail, it’s a matter of when.” So, my general rule of thumb, is that when you get a new machine, also get a new back up drive. This doesn’t mean you have to throw your old one away. I suggest that you put the date of the most current backup, and the word “archive” on a label, and store it away until you are sure that you have everything transferred to the new machine. Currently, there are two kinds of hard drives commonly used, Hard Disk Drives (HDD) and Solid-State Drives (SSD). Solid-state drives are much faster, but also much more expensive. Hard disk drives are very reasonable. You can get a 2 TB one for under $70. It’s a small investment to make sure that your data is backed up. And if you are using the external drive to back up your machine, you don’t particularly need a fast hard drive. An SSD is useful if you are accessing files from the external drive to use on your machine, for example, photos, videos, or music. The data transfer rate is much faster, but in your case not necessary. To use one of these hard drives for Time Machine on your Mac, they must be formatted to make them compatible with Mac. Occasionally, you can find some that are already formatted for Mac, but in many cases, you must do it yourself. It’s much easier than it sounds and usually takes less than five minutes. Your computer comes with an application, called Disk Utility. Apple provides instructions for how to do this. When you reformat a hard drive, you are actually erasing it, and then choosing a file format that works best for Mac. If you have OSX 10.13 or later, the format that works best for Time Machine is APFS (Apple File System), and for systems before OSX 10.13, Mac OS Extended (Journaled) is the one to use. Don’t forget, that since your Mac is new, whether or not you bought Apple Care, you can call Apple Support (800-275- 2273) and they can either talk you through it, or log onto your machine, and visually show you the way. articles.text: Becoming a grandparent doesn’t happen to everyone. When it does, it can come at the most unexpected time of life, or it can come after years of readiness and anticipation. Nothing we do can hurry it up or postpone it. Although we know that every family is unique, there is something universal about becoming a grandparent. Grandparents in cultures all over the world share similar hopes and dreams for the health and happiness of their grandchildren. Many work hard to help their adult children tackle all the tasks associated with raising a young family. Grandparents pass on family lore and wisdom every chance they get. And elders try every day to make the world just a little bit better so that their grandchildren inherit a safe and sustainable planet. Since the life stage called Grandparent is one that hits some of us, but not all of us, and may strike anywhere from age 35 to 100, it’s not unusual for a new grandparent to have no close friends or acquaintances that are going through the grandparent stages at the same time. New parents have lots of options such as parent groups, neighborhood get-togethers, and social media, but grandparents may not know where to turn for advice and support. Enter the Grandparent Group. Grandparents can gather together and learn from each other. Similar to a support group, but not necessarily therapeutic, grandparent groups (or meet-ups) offer grandparents a safe and confidential place to share their experiences. It can be wonderful to be able to talk about your grandchildren without fear of boring the listener. And if you’re going through a tough time communicating with your adult children about an issue regarding the little ones, it’s likely that another grandparent in the group can offer strategies that worked for them. In return, you no doubt have a few helpful ideas that you can share with others. Once you’ve stepped into the role of grandparent, no matter when it happens to you, you might want to explore the benefits of a grandparent group in your area. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Pope Paul VI was visiting Colombia, part of a Latin America tour, and the city vibrated with anticipation. I was having breakfast in a hotel dining room, seated at a table covered in white cloth. Colombia was a very Catholic country and I knew the coming days would be momentous. Looking around the large room, I noticed men and women seated at tables leafing through notebooks and talking animatedly. At their feet were portable typewriters in black cases. They were clearly journalists, there to write about the man from Rome. In that moment I wanted to be one of them, to cover this story, to be part of that headline that would soon emerge. I wanted to write stories, help keep the nation’s record and I thought about those days so long ago that I had delivered the newspaper. Blair came to California in 1852 during the Gold Rush at the age of 22 and purchased 600 acres in the Piedmont hills for $750. The Corporation Yard was among the buildings in Piedmont subject to power outages. “Our power didn’t come back on until Thursday or Friday,” said Gonzales. Fifth graders will hear high school athletes read one of the newly donated books, engage in a discussion about the importance of Title IX, and then view a short video of Title IX champion Congresswoman Patsy Mink. “I am thrilled that Piedmont has stepped up to have a conversation about Title IX this year. Last fall the Speaker Series and the Diversity Film Series covered this topic for adult audiences,” said mayor Jen Cavenaugh. “Activities this spring help a younger generation become informed about the impact of Title IX and the opportunities available to them. No Stopping Us Now, the selected Readmont book this year, is based on the author’s high school years, the book follows the story of Louisa who fought to bring her hometown into compliance with the new Title IX law so she could play basketball at her Oregon high school. It is a book about the love of sports and finding one’s own voice. The Recreation Department encourages all kids to try sports through Try It Out Mondays and its annual Play Like a Girl+ event, this year at Witter Field on April 23 from 10:00 a.m - 1:00 p.m. PHS in New York Continued from page 7 extended beyond journalism. It taught us how to be better leaders in all aspects of our lives. [It was] a lot about the importance of confidence when you’re in charge of a large group, but also stressed that respect is needed for a functioning relationship, and for a strong newspaper,” said senior Ava Adarkar, the Campus Editor. Each session cultivated a space for students to meet other journalism students from across the country, allowing them to learn from like-minded individuals. “It was inspiring to see newspapers from other schools and meet advisors from around the country because everyone genuinely cares so much,” Adarkar said. “The sessions and conversations made the class find a better understanding. Everyone expanded their knowledge on the subject, but it felt especially formative in finding your own niche,” said junior Phoenix Nwokedi, a staff writer. This year, students also had the opportunity to meet individuals in the journalism industry. Gady Epstein, The Economist’s China Affairs Editor, shared his story with the class and answered questions about pursuing a career in journalism. “[Epstein] shared about his experiences writing at his high school newspaper and how that contributes to his work today,” said junior Hana Thomas, the TPH web editor. On the Columbia University campus, Anusha Shrivastava, the Associate Dean of Career Development at the Columbia Journalism School, led TPH staff on a tour of the Journalism School. “[The tour] gave me a lens into what pursuing a career in journalism would even look like. Hearing about all the [alumni] and how they’ve used their degrees is inspiring,” Adarkar said. At the end of each day, the staff met to debrief what they learned and discuss how to incorporate new ideas into The Piedmont Highlander. “We all had many new ideas that we were so excited to implement into TPH once we got home,” Thomas said. “Sharing our ideas with each other inspired our staff and got us excited for the remainder of the school year.” Black said that this is one of her main goals in taking students on the trip. “I love that they come back with so many new ideas that they bring from across the country to Piedmont High School,” Black said. Students also had time to explore the city. As a staff they saw the musical comedy Some Like it Hot on Broadway and walked throgh Central Park and Times Square. “Our class was able to bond a lot throughout the trip and understand each other better as both people and journalists. I feel like we were all reminded of why we took the class in the first place, and why our job is so important,” Adarkar said. After one year as a physical therapist at Stanford Children’s Hospital, she worked for 18 years at California State University in Hayward as kinesiology instructor, head women’s basketball coach, and Athletic Director. She was named Coach of the Year in the Cal Pac Conference in 2000- 2001. Lillevand was lured to city government by longtime Piedmont Recreation Director Mark Delventhal and was hired as his replacement in 2014. During this time, she led the Hampton Park renovation project. On her transition to local government from intercollegiate sports, she said, “It was a unique opportunity to be close to home and give back to a city that’s given so much to me, and in particular the Rec. Department,” she said. Five years later, on June 17, 2019, she became the city’s top employee as its City Administrator when Paul Benoit retired. On August 8, 2022, Lillevand announced her intent to retire on her birthday, April 5, 2023. In recent weeks she has been in conversations with her replacement, Rosanna Bayon Moore, who was hired by the City on February 16. “I’m not surprised she’s been so deeply involved in advance of her start date,” said Lillevand. “I think the city’s really lucky to have her and it won’t take long for the community to recognize that.” Reflecting on the difference between athletics and municipal government, Lillevand said, “The coaching role translates well to local government – it’s just a different kind of team. I see everything through the eyes of a coach.” Of her time as City Administrator, Lillevand said that she was “proudest of having navigated the COVID pandemic.
